### Rules

My daughters attend a preschool that provides play based learning. It’s not “Montessori” though more in line with Maria’s philosophy of child centered inquiry than the many childcare centers branded with Montessori. (There’s no copyright so the word has proliferated rampantly.) 

On the tour, the executive director of the school offered that they only have three rules. Respect themselves. Respect others. Respect their stuff. (Paraphrasing.) I’ve heard other parents will say something to the effect of “they have their whole life to exist in environments filled with rules.” 

Spending time in the school, it’s not like there aren’t a lot of rules in the protocol sense: series of steps to reliably ensure coordination. The school is filled with lots of subtle visual cues for kids ages 2-92. Stop signs on classroom doors. Invitations to measure corn growing. Sign ins and little cues to signal snack time, where shoes go, and a zillion little things to keep lots of self directed littles from descending into anarchy. 

Really the place has few *fixed* rules and to me offers a lot of lessons for overly rigid, strictly scheduled schooling. There is ton of rule creation going on all the time. Kids make up rules as they collaboratively invent little games in the spirit of what adults call improv. “Who wants to play boat?” “I’ve got a fishing pole!” (Holds up a stick and a piece of string.) 

There are many formalisms and much longer timelines. Yet countless human institutions all around us descended from that same spirit, including this American experiment in self-government. 

[Steve Jobs once described the same realization about the made-up nature of the rules around us:

"When you grow up you tend to get told that the world is the way it is and your life is just to live your life inside the world. Try not to bash into the walls too much. Try to have a nice family life, have fun, save a little money. That's a very limited life. Life can be much broader once you discover one simple fact, and that is: everything around you that you call life was made up by people that were no smarter than you. And you can change it, you can influence it, you can build your own things that other people can use. Once you learn that, you'll never be the same again."] 

The skills that a play based environment provides are in many ways more critical in the world today. Learning how to self-regulate. How to interact and collaborate with peers. Finding interests and focus to accomplish a task with real world implications (like helping set up for snack). Tasks more associated with “smart-ness” like learning letters, reading, writing and so on benefit from play. Humans are nothing if not social animals, and as our ecology friends remind us, play is how intelligent animals teach their young. 

You can go faster by specializing and leaning on paths laden with “productive” and “work-like” tactics though ultimately I deeply believe that learning benefits from the deeper skills and mastery that play provides. There is also deep value in learning to set goals and working towards them in total, rather than practicing specific pieces of the puzzle, even if those pieces are more intricate, such as a teacher showing a young three year old how to make marks rather than letting a student write how they think makes sense and iteratively course correct. 

To provide a machine metaphor, play based learning provides the opportunity to identify a load, develop a design, build working parts, and provide fuel. Sometimes folks think of play as an escape from work (which is pretty easy to see why as work has consumed modern life). More regimented approaches may have quicker paths to students showing an understanding of specific designs or working parts, though there is deep benefit for giving learners at any age the space to ask “why” along with the freedom to try different “hows” to answer that “why.” 

Not to mention the deep disconnect that can emerge between what students learn in school and how such learning can apply in life. Interrogating what really constitutes an education is increasingly important as the digital revolution gets supercharged with artificial intelligence. Consider the following ideas recently shared by the inimitable Venkatesh Rao. 

> We teach subjects, test knowledge, reward cleverness, and sort people into status hierarchies based on visible performances of smartness. We sometimes teach study skills, concentration techniques, or emotional regulation, but these are usually treated as auxiliary skills rather than the central developmental achievement.

> We largely leave the acquisition of cognitive balance to chance, and then retrospectively and unreliably recognize it as “smarts” or one of several other traits that reveal the presence of balance. Some more reliably than others.
https://substack.com/@contraptions/p-221947100

The full piece is worth a read and contains lots of useful reframes for smarts, computers, and AI. The critical point though is that AI requires more cognitive balance. It's like a motorcycle for the mind, complete with potential for higher consequence error and failure modes. This makes play based learning environments increasingly critical. It also should make us reconsider the learning rat race in places like the US where folks undertake activities with their kids college application in mind in early grades. (Sadly one of those jokes that are not a joke.) 

That reframing maps neatly onto what I see at my daughters' school. Learning to ride your mind as a proverbial bicycle, what is called taming the monkey mind, is something you can only do yourself. Techniques can be shown, paths may be laid in front of you, a deluxe high end bicycle may even be provided. But nobody can pedal for you, and no amount of explanation substitutes for the hours of wobbling. Play is where kids get those hours. Making up a boat game with a stick and a piece of string means deciding where to go, noticing when the game is falling apart, renegotiating the rules with friends, and sticking with it because it matters to the people around you. That's balance and steering. It's the mind learning to carry itself.

The risk in the AI era is handing kids (and adults, for that matter, who although they sometimes forget, are still learning and benefit from play) a garage full of power tools before they've learned to get around. The tools will happily do impressive, awe-inspiring things, and it's tempting to measure learning by how quickly someone produces the output a tool makes easy. But a power tool in the hands of someone with no sense of direction mostly makes faster, louder mistakes. Fluency with the tools comes naturally once the foundation is in place, not the other way around. The tools will keep changing anyway.

What lasts is the trained mind, and it is trained the way a child learns to ride a bicycle, through hours of wobbling that nobody else can do on her behalf. Asking ‘who wants to play boat?’ shows that a child has noticed the world is made up and can be remade. Keeping the boat afloat when a friend wants different rules, or when the stick turns out to be a poor fishing pole, shows that she has the balance to build what she imagined. If the rules around us really were made up by people no smarter than us, then we have just been handed the most powerful tools in human history for remaking them. How well we use those tools will depend less on how fast we can produce output than on whether we learn, ideally early, often and in the company of competing desires, how to stay upright while we steer.
